newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan, Canada, Europe trade chiefs to meet.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan, Canada, Europe trade chiefs to meet.

text.p: The future of the global trading system and efforts to open markets in a number of sectors are likely to top the agenda of a meeting this week of trade chiefs from the United States, Japan, Canada and Europe.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said the World Trade Organisation and United States desire to see it develop as a forum for continuing trade liberalisation and market opening efforts will be at the centre of discussion when she meets in Seattle on Thursday and Friday with the other members of the so-call Quadrilateral (Quad).

"We want to be sure that the Quad continues to exert a leadership role on the multilateral process and in particular on the formation of the Singapore agenda," Barshefsky said. "That agenda is still very much in flux."
Attending this week's meeting of the Quad will be Canadian Trade Minister Arthur Eggleton, Japanese Industry and Trade Minister Shunpei Tsukahara and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.

The ministers will continue work begun at the last quadrilateral meeting held in Kobe, Japan, in April when the four began discussing what they would like to see on the agenda at the first meeting of WTO ministers to be held in December in Singapore, Barshefsky said.

"Our conception of the WTO is that it is a forum in which continuing trade negotiation and liberalisation can take place and that one need not wait for a new round (of global trade negotiations) to liberalise," Barshefsky told reporters at a briefing last week on the upcoming meeting.

Specifically, Barshefsky said, she would like Quad members to reaffirm support for a global information technology agreement that would eliminate tariffs on a variety of electronic products such as semiconductors, computers, software and telephone equipment.

The United States has accused the European Union of backing away from earlier commitments on the global technology agreement and Barshefsky is likely to discuss the issue when she meets individually with Europe's Brittan.

The Quad ministers are also likely to discuss global negotiations on telecommunications and financial services, both of which ran into trouble after the United States complained that its trading partners failed to make sufficient offers to open up their markets.
"With rspect to all of these negotiations the ministers are going to need to be clearer on how to put together the right kinds of agreements," Barshefsky said.
In addition, Barshefsky said she hopes to discuss an intitiative to curb bribery and corruption though a global agreement to open up government procurement practices to more public scrutiny.
"By far and away, bribery and corruption in government procurement is the single largest problem facing businesses," Barshefsky said.
Barshefsky is also expected to hold bilateral discussions with Eggleton and Tsukahara.
